representations.text: March 30–April 12 remained close to the preceding 28-day baseline, with no missing metrics. Mean sleep was 471.7 versus 470.6 minutes, steps 7,923 versus 7,938, active time 56.2 versus 54.7 minutes, and low movement 446.8 versus 449.7 minutes. Resting heart rate stayed at 61–63 bpm (mean 61.7 versus 61.8); RMSSD remained 43–47 ms (45.1 versus 44.8), with smaller daily fluctuations. Steps trended mildly downward (22/day), while low movement rose 0.7 minute/day; both stayed within baseline ranges. Sleep briefly shortened to 463 minutes on April 8, returning to 476 the next day. Sleep starts remained 22:42–22:57, with waking fixed at 07:00. Weekday/weekend sleep and steps were similar; baseline weekend differences in active time and low movement narrowed. Activity remained one continuous 21:00 session lasting 50–60 minutes; daytime low movement comprised ten roughly 44–47-minute bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Activity versus next-wake-date sleep showed essentially no relationship (r=0.05, 13 pairs); heart rate/RMSSD and steps/active-time relationships were weak.

During March 30–April 12, RMSSD had an isolated April 5 drop to 23 ms versus the preceding 28-day range of 43–47 ms and mean 45.3. It returned to 43 the next day and stayed 43–46 thereafter. This lowered the window mean to 43.1, while the median remained 45; the weekend mean of 39.3 reflects this single Sunday dip. Heart rate that day was 57 bpm, within its baseline range. Overall resting heart rate decreased slightly, 56.3 to 55.8 bpm, continuing a mild downward trend. Sleep averaged 467.7 versus 470.9 minutes, with starts about three minutes later and waking unchanged at 07:00; the baseline weekend sleep advantage largely disappeared. Steps averaged 7,954 versus 8,066, active time 54.9 versus 55.1 minutes, and low movement 453.1 versus 451.1 minutes, without sustained departures. Activity remained a continuous 21:00 session; low movement comprised ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. Activity had no relationship with next-wake-date sleep (r=-0.02, 13 pairs). Heart rate/RMSSD correlation was moderately negative (r=-0.41), including the isolated dip; causation is undetermined. No metrics were missing.

Steps and active minutes fell abruptly on March 30 and remained reduced throughout April 12, across weekdays and weekends, without recovery. Compared with the preceding 28-day baseline, steps averaged 2,321 versus 7,998 (71% lower), with every day at 2,086–2,500; active time averaged 4.9 versus 55.2 minutes (91% lower), ranging 0–10. March 30 and April 8 recorded zero active minutes with no activity interval; other days had one 21:00 bout lasting 2–10 minutes, versus baseline continuous 50–60-minute bouts. All metrics were present with 720 daytime wear minutes daily. Low movement stayed similar (447.5 versus 450.5 minutes), comprising ten daytime bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Sleep remained near baseline (469.4 versus 470.5 minutes), with starts 22:42–22:58 and waking at 07:00; it fluctuated but trended slightly longer. Resting heart rate stayed 55–57 bpm (56.3 versus 56.1); RMSSD averaged 44.8 versus 45.3 ms and trended upward. Thus the movement reduction accompanied little change elsewhere. Activity/next-wake-date sleep association was modest (r=0.32, 13 pairs); heart rate/RMSSD was inverse (r=-0.59), without establishing causation.

Resting heart rate rose abruptly at the March 30 window boundary and stayed elevated for all 14 days through April 12, without returning to the preceding 28-day baseline: mean 61.7 versus 51.8 bpm (+9.9, 19%), with nonoverlapping ranges of 61–63 versus 51–53. The increase appeared on weekdays and weekends, with little further trend. RMSSD remained stable at 43–47 ms (mean 45.1 versus 44.8), without a corresponding sustained decline. Sleep averaged 471.7 versus 470.6 minutes, with starts 22:42–22:57 and waking fixed at 07:00. Sleep shortened locally to 463 minutes on April 8, returning to 476 the next day. Steps averaged 7,923 versus 7,938, active time 56.2 versus 54.7 minutes, and low movement 446.8 versus 449.7 minutes. Steps trended mildly downward while low movement rose slightly, within baseline ranges; weekday/weekend differences were small. Activity remained one continuous 21:00 bout lasting 50–60 minutes; low movement comprised ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. Activity versus next-wake-date sleep was unrelated (r=0.05, 13 pairs), and heart rate/RMSSD association was weak. No metrics were missing.
